title: Advanced Connectivity: Fibre, 5G and Satellites
summary: How data really travels: copper, fibre-optic and wireless transmission, full-fibre broadband, how mobile networks evolved from 1G to 5G and 6G, satellite internet, and the race to connect everyone.
learn: The main transmission media and when each is used
How fibre optics carry data as light
How mobile networks work and how 1G to 5G evolved
What 5G makes possible and what 6G might bring
How satellite internet works, including low Earth orbit constellations
What the digital divide is and how it can be closed
intro: Every video call, game and download travels as light through glass, radio waves through the air or signals bounced off satellites. In this topic you'll find out how each kind of connection works, why Northern Ireland has some of the best full-fibre coverage in the UK, what 5G really changes, how satellites can deliver internet to the middle of the ocean, and why millions of people are still left offline.

pages.title: Transmission media
pages.spec: Compare copper cable, fibre-optic cable and wireless as transmission media
pages.summary: Data travels through transmission media: electrical signals in copper cables, pulses of light in fibre-optic cables, or radio waves through the air. Each has different speed, range, cost and reliability, so networks combine them.
pages.starter: List every way your data might travel between your phone and a video on a server in America.
sc: I can name three transmission media
I can compare them for speed, range, cost and reliability
I can choose suitable media for different situations

b: Copper: electrical signals through metal wires (old phone lines, Ethernet)
Fibre optic: pulses of light through thin strands of glass
Wireless: radio waves through the air (Wi-Fi, 4G/5G, satellite)
Your data usually uses all three on one journey
Bandwidth: how much data can be sent per second (megabits per second, Mbps)
Latency: the delay before data arrives (milliseconds, ms)
High bandwidth = fast downloads; low latency = responsive games and calls
Different media are better at different things
Fibre: huge bandwidth, long distances, but costly to install
Copper: cheap and already everywhere, but slower over distance
Wireless: mobile and flexible, but affected by walls, distance and interference

blocks.text: Transmission media
**[[transmission media]]** are the materials or methods that carry data from one place to another.

blocks.caption: Comparing transmission media
head: Medium
How data travels
Strengths
Weaknesses
rows: Cheap; already installed in most buildings
Signal weakens over distance; can be affected by electrical interference
Pulses of light through thin glass strands
Huge bandwidth; long distances; not affected by electrical interference
Expensive to install; fragile if bent sharply
No cables; lets you move around
Weakens with distance and walls; shared with other users; less secure

blocks.text: Bandwidth and latency

**[[bandwidth]]** is the amount of data that can be sent per second, usually measured in **megabits per second (Mbps)** or **gigabits per second (Gbps)**. **[[latency]]** is the delay before data starts to arrive, measured in **milliseconds (ms)**. Downloading a film needs high bandwidth; online gaming and video calls need low latency.

blocks.title: Download time
blocks.context: A 2 GB game update (16,000 megabits) downloads over a 100 Mbps connection.
steps: Time = data ÷ bandwidth
= 16,000 megabits ÷ 100 Mbps
= 160 seconds
blocks.answer: About 2 minutes 40 seconds (in practice a bit longer, because connections rarely reach their full speed).

blocks.text: Remember 1 byte = 8 bits. Internet speeds are in megaBITS per second, but file sizes are usually in megaBYTES, so multiply the file size by 8.

blocks.title: Match the medium
steps: Read the six scenario cards (e.g. "a cable under the Atlantic", "a fitness tracker", "a school's main network link").
Choose the best transmission medium for each and give one reason.
Calculate how long a 1 GB file takes to download at 50 Mbps and at 900 Mbps.

q.q: Which medium did you choose for "a cable under the Atlantic" and "a fitness tracker", and why?
q.a: Fibre for the Atlantic (huge bandwidth over very long distances); wireless (Bluetooth) for the fitness tracker (it moves around with you and needs little data).

check.q: How does data travel through a fibre-optic cable?
What does bandwidth measure?
o: How much data can be sent per second

check.q: What does latency measure?
Which medium is NOT affected by electrical interference?
check.why: Light isn't affected by electrical noise.

practice.q: Explain the difference between bandwidth and latency.
practice.a: Bandwidth is the amount of data that can be transmitted per second (1); latency is the delay before data arrives (1).

practice.q: Compare fibre-optic cable and wireless for connecting a school's computers.
practice.a: Fibre: higher bandwidth/more reliable/not affected by interference (1) but costly and fixed (1); wireless: flexible/mobile/no cabling but slower, affected by walls/interference/less secure (1).

pages.title: Light in glass: full fibre
pages.spec: Explain how fibre-optic cables carry data and describe full-fibre broadband
pages.summary: Fibre optics send pulses of light along glass strands, trapped by total internal reflection. Full-fibre broadband (FTTP) runs fibre all the way to the building, giving much faster and more reliable connections than older copper lines.
pages.starter: How can light travel round a corner?
sc: I can describe how light travels in an optical fibre
I can explain the difference between FTTC and FTTP
I can explain why full fibre is important for communities

b: An optical fibre is a strand of glass thinner than a hair
Light bounces along inside it by total internal reflection
Data is sent as pulses of light: on = 1, off = 0
Light in glass travels at about 200,000 km per second
slides.n: Demonstrate total internal reflection with a laser and a stream of water if available, or show a video.

b: FTTC: fibre to the street cabinet, then old copper to your home
FTTP (full fibre): fibre all the way to your home or business
Full fibre is much faster and more reliable, and doesn't slow down over distance
Northern Ireland has some of the best full-fibre coverage in the UK
slides.n: Project Stratum, a Northern Ireland government project, extended full fibre to tens of thousands of rural homes and businesses.

b: Around 99% of international internet traffic travels through subsea cables
Hundreds of cables cross the oceans, some over 10,000 km long
They're about as thick as a garden hose in deep water
Damage from ship anchors or sabotage is a real risk

blocks.text: How fibre optics work

An optical fibre is a strand of very pure glass, thinner than a human hair. Light sent into one end bounces off the inside walls, trapped by **[[total internal reflection]]**, so it follows the fibre even round gentle bends. Data is sent as extremely fast pulses of light, with on and off representing 1 and 0. Light in glass travels at about 200,000 km per second, about two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum.
FTTC and FTTP

blocks.caption: Types of broadband
head: Type
How it works
Typical speed
rows: Old telephone wires all the way
Up to about 24 Mbps, slower far from the exchange
Fibre to the street cabinet, copper from cabinet to home
Fibre all the way into the building
Up to 1,000 Mbps (1 Gbps) or more

blocks.text: Full fibre doesn't slow down with distance the way copper does, so it's especially important for rural areas. Thanks to schemes such as **Project Stratum**, Northern Ireland has some of the best full-fibre coverage in the UK, including in many rural parts of Fermanagh.
Subsea cables

About 99% of international internet traffic travels through **[[subsea cable|subsea cables]]** lying on the ocean floor, not through satellites. Hundreds of these fibre cables link the continents. Several land on the coast of Ireland, connecting Europe and North America. Because so much depends on them, damage from ship anchors, earthquakes or sabotage is a serious concern.

blocks.title: Broadband detective
steps: Use the broadband checker your teacher shows (e.g. Ofcom's coverage checker) to look up the school's postcode (not your home address).
Record what types of broadband are available and the maximum speeds.
Compare with one city postcode and one remote rural postcode your teacher gives you.
Explain the differences.

q.q: Record the results for the three postcodes.
q.a: Answers depend on the postcodes, e.g. school: full fibre up to 1 Gbps; city: full fibre and cable; remote: FTTC up to 30 Mbps or satellite only.

q.q: Explain why full fibre matters for a rural farm or business.
q.a: It gives fast, reliable internet that doesn't slow down over long distances, so farms and businesses can use online services, video calls, smart sensors and cloud tools as well as city businesses can.

check.q: How does light stay inside an optical fibre?
check.why: Light bounces off the inside walls.

check.q: What does FTTP mean?
o: Fibre all the way to the premises

check.q: How does most international internet traffic travel?
Why is full fibre better than FTTC for homes far from the cabinet?
o: Fibre doesn't slow down over distance like copper

practice.q: Describe how data is sent through a fibre-optic cable.
practice.a: Data is sent as pulses of light (on/off = 1/0) (1); light is kept inside the glass by total internal reflection (1).

practice.q: Explain why damage to subsea cables could be a serious problem.
practice.a: Most international internet traffic travels through them (1), so damage could slow or cut communication between countries/affect banking, business etc. (1).

pages.title: Mobile networks: 1G to 5G
pages.spec: Describe how mobile networks work and how each generation improved
pages.summary: Mobile networks divide areas into cells, each served by a mast that connects phones using radio waves. Each generation, from 1G to 5G, has added new abilities and higher speeds: from voice calls to texts, mobile internet, video streaming and now huge numbers of connected devices.
pages.starter: Your phone works on a moving train. How does it stay connected as you pass from town to town?
sc: I can explain how a cellular network works
I can describe what each generation added
I can explain the trade-off between range and speed

b: The country is divided into areas called cells
Each cell has a mast (base station) with antennas
Your phone talks to the nearest mast using radio waves
As you move, it is handed over to the next mast
1G (1980s): analogue voice calls
2G (1990s): digital calls and text messages
3G (2000s): mobile internet
4G (2010s): fast data, video streaming and apps
5G (2019 onwards): very fast, low latency, many more devices
Mobile networks use radio frequencies called spectrum
Low frequencies: travel far and through walls, but carry less data
High frequencies: carry lots of data, but short range
Governments auction spectrum to mobile companies (Ofcom in the UK)

blocks.text: How mobile networks work

A **[[cellular network]]** divides an area into many small zones called cells. Each cell is served by a **[[mast]]** (base station) with antennas that send and receive radio waves. Your phone connects to the nearest mast, which is linked by cables (often fibre) to the rest of the network and the internet. As you travel, your phone is passed from one mast to the next without the call dropping. This is called a **[[handover]]**.
The generations

blocks.caption: Mobile generations
head: Generation
Roughly when
What it added
rows: Digital calls and SMS text messages
Fast data: video streaming, apps, social media
Much faster, much lower latency, millions of connected devices

blocks.text: UK networks have been switching off 3G to reuse its radio frequencies for 4G and 5G, and 2G is due to follow by around 2033.
Spectrum: the range-speed trade-off
Mobile networks use parts of the radio **[[spectrum]]**. In the UK, Ofcom manages it and auctions it to mobile companies.

blocks.title: Low or high frequency?
items: Low frequencies travel further and through walls, but carry less data: good for rural coverage
High frequencies carry much more data, but over short distances and are blocked easily: good for crowded city centres and stadiums
5G uses both, plus very high "millimetre wave" frequencies in a few busy places

blocks.title: Cell planner
steps: Use the map of a (fictional) town and countryside your teacher gives you, with a stadium, a town centre, farms and a lough.
You have six masts: three low-frequency (big range, less data) and three high-frequency (small range, lots of data).
Place them to give everyone coverage and enough capacity for match day at the stadium.
Explain your choices.

q.q: Where did you place the high-frequency masts and why?
q.a: In the stadium and town centre, because lots of people are packed together using data, and high frequencies carry lots of data over short distances.

q.q: Where did you place the low-frequency masts and why?
q.a: In the countryside, because they reach further and through walls and trees, giving coverage to scattered farms with fewer masts.

check.q: What is a cell in a mobile network?
o: An area served by one mast

check.q: What is a handover?
o: Passing your connection from one mast to the next as you move
check.why: It keeps calls going on the move.

check.q: Which generation introduced text messages?
Why do rural areas often use lower-frequency signals?
o: They travel further and through obstacles

practice.q: Describe how a mobile phone stays connected while travelling on a train.
practice.a: Area divided into cells each with a mast (1); phone connects to the nearest mast by radio waves (1); connection is handed over to the next mast as it moves (1).

practice.q: Explain the trade-off between low-frequency and high-frequency radio signals in mobile networks.
practice.a: Low frequency: longer range/through walls but less data (1); high frequency: more data but shorter range/blocked easily (1).

pages.title: 5G and the road to 6G
pages.spec: Explain what 5G makes possible and describe the ideas behind 6G
pages.summary: 5G offers faster speeds, much lower latency and the ability to connect huge numbers of devices, enabling new uses in health, transport and industry. Researchers are already developing 6G, expected around 2030, which may combine communication with sensing and AI.
pages.starter: A surgeon in Belfast operates a robot in a hospital in Enniskillen. What would they need from the network?
sc: I can describe three improvements of 5G over 4G
I can give examples of uses that need 5G
I can describe what 6G might bring

b: Speed: peak speeds many times faster than 4G
Latency: as low as a few milliseconds in ideal conditions
Capacity: up to a million devices per square kilometre
Reliability for critical uses
Smart factories with wireless robots
Remote healthcare and monitoring
Connected and self-driving vehicles talking to each other
Smart farming: sensors on soil, livestock and machinery
Researchers expect 6G around 2030
Even higher frequencies and speeds
The network itself could sense its surroundings: detecting movement, mapping rooms
AI built in to manage the network automatically
slides.n: 6G is still being researched and standardised, so details will change. Good opportunity to discuss how predictions can be wrong.

blocks.text: What does 5G improve?
**[[5G]]** is the fifth generation of mobile network.

blocks.caption: 4G and 5G compared
head: Feature
4G
5G
rows: Hundreds of Mbps, up to several Gbps in ideal conditions
As low as a few ms in ideal conditions

blocks.text: **[[low latency|Low latency]]** is one of 5G's biggest changes. A tiny delay matters for things like remote-controlled machines, multiplayer games, and vehicles warning each other about hazards.
Network slicing

**[[network slicing]]** lets one physical 5G network be divided into separate virtual networks, each with its own guaranteed performance. One "slice" might give emergency services priority and reliability, while another serves smartphones and another serves thousands of low-power sensors.
Uses of 5G

blocks.title: Where 5G helps
items: Industry: wireless robots and sensors in smart factories
Health: remote monitoring, ambulances sending live video to hospitals
Transport: vehicles and traffic lights sharing information
Farming: sensors monitoring soil, crops and animals across large areas
Events: thousands of fans using phones in one stadium

blocks.text: 6G

Researchers are already working on **[[6G]]**, expected around 2030. Ideas include even faster speeds using very high frequencies, networks that can **sense** their surroundings like a radar (detecting movement or mapping a room), and AI built into the network to manage it automatically. 6G standards are still being agreed, so what it will really look like may change.

Claims that 5G causes illness have been investigated by scientists and health organisations, which found no evidence of harm at the levels used. Radio waves used by mobile networks are low-energy and well within international safety limits.

blocks.title: 5G innovation pitch
steps: Choose one area of life in Fermanagh: farming, healthcare, tourism around the lakes, or transport.
Design a new service that needs 5G. Explain which 5G feature it depends on: speed, low latency or many devices.
Identify one challenge (cost, coverage, privacy).
Pitch it in 60 seconds.

q.q: Describe your service and the 5G feature it depends on.
q.a: E.g. "Smart herd: collars on cattle report location and health to the farmer's phone. It needs 5G's ability to connect many low-power devices over a large area."

q.q: What challenge would your service face, and how could it be solved?
q.a: E.g. "Poor coverage in remote fields: use low-frequency 5G masts with long range, or combine with satellite."

check.q: Which is a key improvement of 5G over 4G?
check.why: Low latency is a major change.

check.q: About how many devices per square kilometre can 5G support?
What is network slicing?
o: Dividing one 5G network into separate virtual networks with different performance

check.q: When is 6G expected?

practice.q: Describe three improvements that 5G offers over 4G.
practice.a: Any three: faster speeds (1); lower latency (1); more devices/capacity (1); network slicing/reliability (1).

practice.q: Explain why low latency is important for remote surgery.
practice.a: The surgeon's movements must reach the robot instantly (1), as any delay could cause dangerous mistakes (1).

pages.title: Internet from space
pages.spec: Explain how satellite internet works and compare geostationary and low Earth orbit satellites
pages.summary: Satellite internet sends signals between a dish and satellites in space. Geostationary satellites are far away, causing high latency, while new low Earth orbit constellations of thousands of satellites give much lower latency, but raise concerns about space debris and astronomy.
pages.starter: You're on a ship in the middle of the Atlantic. How could you get online?
sc: I can describe how satellite internet works
I can compare GEO and LEO satellites
I can evaluate the benefits and problems of satellite constellations

b: A dish at your home sends signals to a satellite
The satellite relays them to a ground station connected to the internet
Works almost anywhere with a clear view of the sky
Used by ships, planes, remote homes and disaster zones
Geostationary (GEO): about 36,000 km up, stays above one spot
Signals travel so far that latency is about 600 ms round trip
Low Earth orbit (LEO): about 500-2,000 km up, moving fast
Much lower latency (about 20-50 ms), but needs thousands of satellites
Starlink and others have launched thousands of LEO satellites
Brought internet to remote areas, ships and war zones
Concerns: space debris, collisions, bright trails spoiling astronomy
One company controlling vital connections raises questions

blocks.text: How satellite internet works

A dish (or terminal) sends radio signals up to a satellite, which relays them down to a ground station connected to the internet, and back again. It works almost anywhere with a clear view of the sky: remote farms, islands, ships, aeroplanes and disaster areas where cables are damaged.
GEO and LEO

blocks.caption: Comparing satellite orbits
head: Feature
Geostationary (GEO)
Low Earth orbit (LEO)
rows: Stays above the same spot on Earth
A few cover most of the world
Thousands, to always have one overhead

blocks.text: A **[[geostationary orbit]]** is so far away that signals take a noticeable time to travel up and back, causing high latency. **[[low Earth orbit]]** satellites are much closer, so latency is far lower, but each one is only overhead for a few minutes, so you need a huge **[[satellite constellation]]** of them, handing over from one to the next.

blocks.title: Why GEO is slow to respond
blocks.context: Radio signals travel at about 300,000 km per second. A request goes up to a GEO satellite and down to a ground station, then the reply comes back the same way.
steps: Distance: 36,000 km up + 36,000 km down = 72,000 km each way
Request and reply: 72,000 × 2 = 144,000 km
Time = 144,000 ÷ 300,000 ≈ 0.48 seconds, before any processing delay
blocks.answer: About half a second of delay just from distance, which is why GEO internet feels laggy for games and video calls.

blocks.text: Problems and concerns
Low Earth orbit constellations have brought fast internet to remote areas, ships and even war zones. But they also raise concerns:

items: **[[space debris]]**: dead satellites and fragments can collide, creating more debris
Astronomy: bright satellite trails can spoil telescope images
Control: a few private companies controlling vital connections can be a risk

blocks.title: Choose a connection
steps: Read the five profiles: a Fermanagh farm, a cruise ship, a research station in Antarctica, a flat in Belfast and a gamer on a Scottish island.
For each, recommend full fibre, 5G, GEO satellite or LEO satellite, with a reason.
Calculate the minimum latency for LEO using a height of 550 km (up and down, there and back).

q.q: Give your recommendation and reason for the gamer on a Scottish island.
q.a: LEO satellite (if no fibre is available): much lower latency than GEO, so online games are playable; full fibre would be best if available.
550 × 2 = 1,100 km each way; × 2 for request and reply = 2,200 km; 2,200 ÷ 300,000 ≈ 0.0073 s ≈ 7 ms, before processing and network delays.

check.q: About how high is a geostationary satellite?
Why does GEO satellite internet have high latency?
Why do LEO constellations need thousands of satellites?
o: Each satellite is only overhead for a short time
To spell words in the sky

check.q: Which is a concern about large satellite constellations?

practice.q: Compare geostationary and low Earth orbit satellites for internet access.
practice.a: GEO much higher (~36,000 km) vs LEO (~500-2,000 km) (1); GEO has high latency, LEO low latency (1); GEO needs few satellites to cover Earth, LEO needs thousands (1).

practice.q: Give one benefit and one problem of satellite internet constellations.
practice.a: Benefit: internet anywhere, e.g. remote areas, ships, disaster zones (1); problem: space debris/astronomy/private control/cost (1).

pages.title: Connecting everyone
pages.spec: Describe the digital divide and evaluate ways to connect more people
pages.summary: The digital divide is the gap between people who have good internet access and skills and those who don't. It is caused by location, cost, skills and disability, and affects education, jobs and health. Governments, companies and communities are trying to close it.
pages.starter: During the pandemic, schools taught online. Who might have been left out, and why?
sc: I can explain what the digital divide is
I can describe its causes and effects
I can evaluate solutions to close it

b: About a third of the world's people still don't use the internet
Rural areas often have slower connections
Cost of devices and data is a barrier for some families
Skills, confidence and accessibility matter too
slides.n: The International Telecommunication Union estimated about 2.6 billion people were offline in 2024.

b: School: homework, revision sites, online classes
Work: job applications, remote working
Health and money: GP appointments, banking, benefits
People without access fall further behind
Infrastructure: full fibre, rural masts, satellites
Affordability: social tariffs, device donation schemes
Skills: libraries, community classes, school support
Resilience: networks that keep working in storms and emergencies

blocks.text: The digital divide

The **[[digital divide]]** is the gap between people who have good internet access, devices and skills and those who don't. Around the world, roughly a third of people still don't use the internet. Even in the UK, some people can't afford broadband, live where connections are poor, or lack the skills or confidence to get online.

blocks.caption: Causes of the digital divide
head: Cause
Example
rows: A remote farmhouse with slow broadband and no mobile signal
A family who can't afford a laptop or monthly broadband
An older person who has never used a smartphone
Websites that don't work with a screen reader

blocks.text: Why it matters

More and more of life happens online: schoolwork, job applications, banking, GP appointments and government services. People without good access risk falling further behind, which increases inequality.
Closing the gap
**[[digital inclusion]]** means making sure everyone can use the internet and digital technology. Solutions include:

items: **Infrastructure**: full fibre, extra rural masts and satellite services.
**Affordability**: cheaper "social tariffs" for people on low incomes, and schemes that donate refurbished devices.
**Skills**: free classes in libraries and community centres, and support in schools.
**Accessible design**: websites and apps that work for everyone.

blocks.text: Resilience

**[[resilience]]** means a network can keep working, or recover quickly, when something goes wrong, such as a storm bringing down cables, a power cut or a damaged subsea cable. Resilient networks have backups: more than one route, battery power at masts, and alternatives such as satellite links.

blocks.title: Close the gap
steps: Your group is given a budget of £10 million to reduce the digital divide in a rural county like Fermanagh.
Choose how to spend it across infrastructure, affordability, skills and accessibility (use the cost cards).
Justify your choices: who benefits, and how many people?
Present your plan in 90 seconds.

q.q: Summarise your spending plan and the reasons for it.
q.a: E.g. £5m on extra masts and fibre for the most remote areas; £2m on refurbished laptops for families on low incomes; £2m on library digital skills classes; £1m on making council websites accessible. Reasons should link spending to the main causes of the divide.

q.q: Which group of people do you think is most affected by the digital divide, and why?
q.a: A reasoned answer, e.g. older people in rural areas: poorer connections plus less confidence with technology, at the same time as more services move online.

check.q: What is the digital divide?
o: The gap between people with good internet access and skills and those without

check.q: Which is a cause of the digital divide?
o: The cost of devices and broadband

check.q: What is digital inclusion?
o: Including more apps on a phone
Making sure everyone can use digital technology

check.q: What does network resilience mean?
o: Keeping working or recovering quickly when something goes wrong

practice.q: Describe three causes of the digital divide.
practice.a: Any three: location/poor rural infrastructure (1); cost of devices/broadband (1); lack of skills/confidence (1); accessibility barriers (1).

practice.q: Evaluate one way of reducing the digital divide.
practice.a: Describes a method (1); explains a benefit (1); gives a limitation or judgement, e.g. satellites reach remote homes but cost more / skills classes help but need people to attend (1).

An orbit about 36,000 km high where a satellite stays above the same point on Earth.
An orbit about 500-2,000 km high where satellites circle Earth quickly.
